implementation_notes: Swift's standard library ships atomics but no queue: since Swift 6 the Synchronization module provides Atomic<Value> (noncopyable) with explicit memory orderings, which is enough to build a bounded index ring whose head/tail tickets and per-slot sequence words are claimed with compareExchange - index arithmetic needs no pointer reclamation, which is exactly why the ring is the workable Swift shape. The classic node-linked structure is therefore replaced by an index ring plus a Mutex or actor for the waiting path, not by a library queue; Apple's proposal and the swift-atomics README both warn that atomics are a last resort for library authors. Node-based queues are not recommended: ARC does not manage UnsafeMutablePointer nodes and no hazard-pointer/epoch facility exists, leaving reclamation to the caller.
pitfalls: Swift's strict concurrency does not understand lock-free invariants: shared mutable state must be audited as @unchecked Sendable or hidden behind an actor.
There is no standard safe reclamation for UnsafeMutablePointer nodes; prefer index rings, or wrap nodes in Unmanaged with a scheme you own and test.
Swift Atomics is largely superseded by Synchronization.Atomic in Swift 6, so a new package dependency is only for toolchains older than 6.0.

variants.name: swift-atomics ManagedAtomic (pre-Swift 6 toolchains)
variants.implementation_notes: For Swift 5.7-5.9 toolchains the same ring is built on the apple/swift-atomics package: ManagedAtomic<Int> carries the tickets and sequences with the same explicit orderings, and AtomicReference covers the rare case where a pointer must be swapped (it implements atomic strong references on top of double-word operations). The package README states that all its atomic operations are lock-free but not wait-free and that Swift 6's Synchronization.Atomic supersedes it, so treat this variant as the compatibility path, not the target state.
pitfalls: Mixing ManagedAtomic and the Swift 6 stdlib Atomic in one module doubles the storage representations - pick one per toolchain.
Atomic strong references are relatively expensive; prefer index-based rings when the payload can live in an array.
